Pregnancy

Recurrent miscarriage: choosing investigations and care

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Repeated miscarriage can leave you wanting both an explanation and a clear plan. An assessment can look for findings that would change your care, although it may not identify a definite cause. The useful question is not simply how many tests are available, but what each result would mean for you. You deserve careful explanations, time for decisions and support throughout that process.

Ask about assessment after repeated losses

There is no single international definition. ACOG and ASRM use two or more losses; ASRM’s 2026 definition includes pregnancies confirmed by a urine or blood pregnancy test and excludes confirmed ectopic and molar pregnancies. RCOG’s patient information describes three or more early miscarriages. Its definition does not require consecutive losses: a live birth between miscarriages does not erase the history.

Ask your clinician when investigation or referral is appropriate after two losses, or sooner for a concerning medical history or later loss. Bring the details even if a pregnancy ended before a scan. The service can explain which events it counts and which pathway applies. You do not have to meet a research definition before asking for emotional support or assessment of current symptoms.

Make the first appointment a review of the whole history

Prepare a short timeline: positive tests, approximate pregnancy dates, scans, how each loss was confirmed, any treatment and any laboratory results. Include live births, ectopic or molar pregnancies and relevant family history. Bring your medicines and supplements list. If there is a partner, ask how their health and reproductive history will be included; repeated loss is not automatically attributable to one person.

Ask the team to separate what is already known from what remains uncertain. For each proposed investigation, write down the question it answers, when it should be done, possible results and the next decision. Ask who will explain the results and arrange follow-up. This can make a complicated appointment more manageable and helps avoid repeating investigations simply because records are scattered.

Clarify whose chromosomes are being tested

Many miscarriages involve a chance error in the embryo’s chromosome number, often despite both parents having normal chromosomes. Age affects the likelihood of these errors. A chromosome finding in pregnancy tissue is different from a chromosome rearrangement in a parent, and neither automatically establishes that the same explanation applies to every previous loss.

A parental karyotype examines chromosome number and structure, usually in blood cells. Selected results may lead to genetic counselling about inheritance and future options. Ask whether testing concerns the pregnancy, one parent or both, and what a normal result cannot exclude. Detailed sperm DNA testing is another question; it should not be confused with a parental karyotype or assumed necessary for everyone.

Distinguish APS from a general “clotting problem”

Antiphospholipid syndrome, or APS, can be relevant to repeated loss. Diagnosis combines an appropriate clinical history with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies, generally confirmed on samples at least 12 weeks apart. One positive result does not by itself establish APS or prove the cause of a miscarriage. APS, inherited thrombophilia and systemic lupus are not interchangeable diagnoses.

For people with obstetric APS, specialist-selected low-dose aspirin and heparin can improve pregnancy outcomes. That does not justify taking them after any loss or positive antibody test. Routine anticoagulants have not shown benefit for unexplained recurrent miscarriage or inherited thrombophilia alone. Ask what diagnosis supports the prescription and how it will be monitored; do not start or stop prescribed treatment on your own.

Thyroid antibodies and thyroid function are different findings

Thyroid assessment looks at hormone function, often beginning with thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH. Known thyroid disease needs appropriate management. Guidelines differ on antibody screening: RCOG’s 2023 information includes it, whereas ASRM’s 2026 opinion does not recommend routine thyroid-antibody screening for recurrent loss. A positive antibody result is an association, not proof that antibodies caused an individual miscarriage.

The 2022 T4LIFE trial studied 187 women with thyroid peroxidase antibodies, normal thyroid function and at least two losses. Levothyroxine did not improve live-birth rates compared with placebo. Recruitment stopped early, so the estimates have uncertainty; the result nevertheless does not support routine thyroid hormone solely for antibodies when function is normal. It does not apply to someone who needs treatment for an underactive thyroid. Ask which situation your results describe.

Use uterine imaging to identify a specific question

Imaging may examine the shape and cavity of the uterus. A septum, some fibroids or scar tissue may be relevant, but an imaging finding is not automatically the explanation for every loss. Ask what was seen, whether further imaging would clarify it, and how strongly it is linked to your history before moving from a scan result to a procedure.

Surgery is a decision with uncertainty. In a small 2021 randomised trial involving 80 women with a uterine septum and a history of fertility problems, pregnancy loss or preterm birth, septum removal did not improve live birth compared with waiting. The study was limited and included different histories. Guidelines still allow discussion of surgery in selected circumstances. Ask about likely benefit, risks, alternatives and what happens if you choose monitoring.

A later loss may need a different specialist pathway

If a previous pregnancy ended later, discuss that timing explicitly. A cervix that opens too early is one possible issue, but it is not the explanation for every second-trimester loss. RCOG advises early specialist review in a subsequent pregnancy after a miscarriage beyond 16 weeks. The earlier records can help the team decide whether cervical surveillance belongs in your plan.

Some people are offered ultrasound measurements, progesterone for a specific preterm-birth indication, or a cervical stitch called cerclage. These are selected according to history and findings, and a stitch has risks and may not prevent loss. There is no universal rule that everyone with repeated miscarriage needs scans from 14 weeks or a stitch. Ask for a personal schedule and the reason for each intervention.

Be cautious about natural-killer-cell and immune add-ons

Natural killer cells are part of the immune system; their name does not mean they are attacking a pregnancy. Blood measurements do not establish how specialised uterine cells function or predict a successful pregnancy. HFEA’s advice on immune add-ons in IVF and ICSI warns about uncertain benefit and potentially serious harms. That advice is separate from treatment prescribed for an established autoimmune disease.

Recurrent-loss guidance is not identical across organisations. ASRM advises against routine immune testing and treatment. ESHRE’s 2022 update conditionally mentions a possible benefit of a particular early, high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin regimen after four or more unexplained losses, based on one trial and with more research needed. This is not validation of commercial NK-cell panels or a general treatment recommendation. Ask a specialist about the exact evidence, eligibility, harms and cost.

Know when progesterone is supported by evidence

Progesterone is not a universal remedy for a history of miscarriage. NICE recommends vaginal micronised progesterone when a scan confirms a pregnancy inside the uterus, there is vaginal bleeding and there has been a previous miscarriage. If a fetal heartbeat is confirmed, its recommended course continues to 16 completed weeks. The assessment comes first because bleeding can have other causes, including ectopic pregnancy.

The evidence concerns a particular preparation and route; vaginal, rectal and oral products should not be assumed equivalent. Ask the clinician whether you meet the criteria, how to use the prescribed product and when to review it. Do not start leftover medication or delay urgent assessment while obtaining it. A further loss is not proof that you failed to request treatment early enough.

An unexplained result still deserves a care plan

Investigations may not reveal a cause that can be treated. This does not mean the losses were imagined, that you caused them, or that another pregnancy cannot succeed. Avoid buying a treatment simply to fill the uncertainty. Ask what evidence shows an improvement in live birth for people with a history like yours, rather than only a change in a laboratory result.

General preparation still matters: discuss existing illness, medicines, smoking and other relevant exposures with your team. Recommended preconception folic acid helps prevent neural-tube defects; it has not been shown to prevent unexplained recurrent miscarriage. Support for healthy routines should not become a claim that perfect behaviour guarantees a baby. Ask about any proposed restriction rather than assuming all ordinary activity must stop.

Plan support and the next pregnancy together

Your outlook depends on your age and complete pregnancy history, including losses, live births and their order, as well as the findings of assessment. A general percentage cannot promise your outcome. Ask what is reasonably known for your circumstances, what remains uncertain and how the plan would change after a new result. You can take time to consider your options.

Arrange a contact plan for a future positive pregnancy test and discuss what monitoring can realistically provide. Support may include reassurance scans, counselling or help with anxiety and grief; these do not guarantee that every loss can be prevented. Partners may need support too. Write down whom to contact between appointments and who will coordinate care if more than one specialist is involved.

Current pregnancy symptoms take priority over planned tests

Seek urgent medical advice for spotting, light bleeding, unusual vaginal discharge or fluid leakage during pregnancy. These symptoms need their own assessment; a previous normal investigation or a planned recurrent-loss appointment does not explain what is happening now. Tell the service your pregnancy history and any current medicines, including prescribed aspirin, heparin or progesterone.

Seek emergency help if vaginal bleeding occurs with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after putting it on also needs emergency help. Do not wait for a scheduled scan, blood-test result or fertility-clinic call before obtaining care for these symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ASRM’s 2026 opinion, RCOG’s 2023 patient information and ESHRE’s 2022 update differ on selected investigations and treatments. The dates describe those publications, not a new edition inferred from an access date.

The T4LIFE and uterine-septum trials address defined patient groups. Their findings should not be extended to untreated thyroid disease or every uterine abnormality.

NICE’s progesterone recommendations apply to a specific bleeding-and-previous-loss situation; immune add-on evidence is not a reason to change treatment for an established autoimmune condition.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to organise questions and records for a recurrent-loss consultation. BeMama cannot determine the cause of a loss, select a prescription or replace assessment of symptoms.

When to seek help

Do not self-prescribe hormones, blood thinners or immune treatments. Pregnancy spotting, light bleeding, unusual discharge or fluid leakage need urgent advice. Bleeding with severe abdominal pain or shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or collapse, or heavy bleeding soaking a pad quickly, needs emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ask about assessment after repeated losses; definitions and referral thresholds differ.
  • Choose investigations according to the question they answer and what a result would change.
  • Treatments for confirmed conditions are different from unproven remedies for unexplained loss.
  • A positive thyroid antibody or immune-cell result does not establish the cause of a miscarriage.
  • A written follow-up plan, emotional support and prompt symptom assessment are all parts of care.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as recurrent miscarriage?

Definitions vary. ACOG and ASRM use two or more losses, while RCOG describes three or more early miscarriages. The losses do not have to be consecutive under RCOG’s definition. Ask which assessment pathway applies to your complete history.

Can I still have a successful pregnancy after repeated losses?

Yes, it remains possible, including when investigations do not find a cause. Your outlook depends on age, the sequence of previous pregnancies and individual findings. Ask for an explanation of your circumstances instead of relying on a general success percentage.

Does a clotting result mean I need aspirin and heparin?

Not automatically. APS requires an appropriate clinical history and persistent antibody findings; inherited clotting conditions are different. Treatment is selected for a clear indication and needs medical supervision. Do not use blood thinners simply because recurrent-loss tests are unexplained.

Do thyroid antibodies cause miscarriage, and should I take thyroid hormone?

Antibodies can be associated with loss but do not establish its cause. In the T4LIFE trial, levothyroxine did not improve live birth in women with antibodies and normal thyroid function. Thyroid disease requiring treatment is a different situation; discuss your actual hormone results.

Should I pay for an NK-cell test?

Ask what useful decision the result could support. Blood NK-cell results do not establish that immune cells caused a loss, and routine immune testing is not recommended by ASRM. Costs and treatment risks deserve discussion before agreeing to an add-on.

Is progesterone offered to everyone after a miscarriage?

No. NICE supports a specified vaginal preparation for bleeding in a scan-confirmed intrauterine pregnancy when there has been a previous miscarriage. Other circumstances need their own assessment. Do not assume different routes or formulations have the same evidence.

Does a uterine septum or a later miscarriage always mean surgery?

No. The precise finding and previous pregnancy details matter. Benefits and risks of septum surgery or a cervical stitch differ, and neither is a guaranteed solution. Ask a specialist which evidence applies to you and whether monitoring is an option.

What should I leave the appointment knowing?

Know which tests are planned and why, who will explain the results, which treatment has a clear indication, whom to contact in a new pregnancy and how to obtain emotional support. Current bleeding or other warning symptoms need prompt care rather than waiting for that plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
